game_chess.name: Chess
game_chess.title: Chess
game_chess.desc: The world's most classic strategy board game.
game_chess.rules: White moves first. Move pieces one at a time to checkmate the opponent's king. A king with no legal moves while in check is checkmate — game over.
game_chess.special1: When neither king nor rook has moved and no pieces stand between them, move the king two squares toward the rook (O-O / O-O-O).
game_chess.special2: After your pawn reaches the 5th rank, it may capture an enemy pawn that just moved two squares beside it.
game_chess.special3: A pawn reaching the last rank automatically promotes to a queen.
game_chess.coach_desc: Click a piece to highlight all legal moves; after each move, AI gives a bilingual tip to help you understand the position.

game_tictactoe.name: Tic-Tac-Toe
game_tictactoe.title: Tic-Tac-Toe
game_tictactoe.desc: 3×3 grid. Connect three in a row to win.
game_tictactoe.rules: 3×3 board, you are ✕ and move first. Players take turns placing marks; the first to line up three in a row, column or diagonal wins.
game_tictactoe.tip1: Open with the center: take the center then a diagonal to control the board.
game_tictactoe.tip2: Defend first: block immediately when the opponent has two in a row.
game_tictactoe.tip3: Double threat: create two lines one move from winning so the opponent can't block both.
game_tictactoe.ai_desc: Easy: random moves. Normal: heuristic + blocks threats. Hard: minimax + perfect play (with optimal play the first player can always force a draw).

game_gomoku.name: Gomoku
game_gomoku.title: Gomoku
game_gomoku.desc: 15×15 board. Connect five in a row to win.
game_gomoku.rules: On a 15×15 board, black moves first. Players alternately place stones on intersections; the first to line up five stones horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins. No forbidden moves.
game_gomoku.tip1: Double-three / open-four: create two open lines the opponent can't block at once to boost your win rate.
game_gomoku.tip2: Defend first: block immediately when the opponent has four in a row (unless you can form an even stronger threat).
game_gomoku.tip3: Control key points: grab the center and star points early to expand your territory.
game_gomoku.ai_desc: Easy: random + simple heuristics. Normal: scoring + shallow search. Hard: threat-space search + locally optimal play.

game_connect4.name: Connect 4
game_connect4.title: Connect 4
game_connect4.desc: 7×6 board with gravity. Connect four in a row to win.
game_connect4.rules: 7 columns × 6 rows with gravity; red goes first. Click ↓ above a column to drop a piece (they stack). The first to connect four in a row, column or diagonal wins. Full columns can't be used.
game_connect4.tip1: Control the center: center columns create the most multi-directional threats.
game_connect4.tip2: Build a double threat: create two lines both one move from winning.
game_connect4.tip3: Defend the height: block above the opponent's develop-ing line before they win.
game_connect4.ai_desc: Easy: random. Normal: immediate win/block + window scoring. Hard: depth-limited negamax + heuristic ordering.

game_othello.name: Othello
game_othello.title: Othello
game_othello.desc: 8×8 flip game. Trap and flip your opponent's pieces.
game_othello.rules: 8×8 board, black goes first; four discs start in the center. Place a disc to trap a line of opponent discs horizontally, vertically or diagonally — all trapped discs flip to your color. Pass if you have no moves. Most discs at the end wins.
game_othello.tip1: Corners > edges > center: a disc on a corner can never be flipped — stay stable. Center discs flip easiest.
game_othello.tip2: Avoid giving corners: don't force yourself into the square next to a corner.
game_othello.tip3: Fewer flips can be better: flipping many at once exposes weak side; pros trade quantity for stability.
game_othello.ai_desc: Easy: random. Normal: positional weights + flip balance. Hard: depth-limited negamax + mobility/frontier weights.

game_checkers.name: Checkers
game_checkers.title: Checkers
game_checkers.desc: Classic 8×8 draughts with forced captures, multi-jumps and kings. vs AI with 3 difficulties.
game_checkers.rules: 8×8 board, black moves first, pieces advance diagonally. Captures are forced; multi-jumps allowed; reaching the far rank crowns a king that may move backward. Lose by immobilization or no pieces.
game_checkers.tip1: Forced captures: you must capture when possible — plan a jump chain to take several at once.
game_checkers.tip2: Crown kings early: kings move backward and become much stronger.
game_checkers.tip3: Control the center: center pieces have more room; first-mover has an edge.
game_checkers.ai_desc: Easy: random + simple heuristics. Normal: scoring + shallow search. Hard: deep search + capture quiescence.
game_checkers.coach_desc: Click a piece to highlight all legal moves; after each move, AI gives a bilingual tip to help you understand the position.

chess.you_black: You play Black, waiting for White
chess.bs1_desc: The opening revolves around the four central squares d4, e4, d5 and e5. Controlling the center maximizes your pieces' range.
chess.bs2_desc: Bring out knights and bishops (minor pieces) before the queen and rooks (major pieces), getting more pieces into the fight.
chess.bs3_desc: Castling protects your king while activating a rook. Castle early to tuck your king into safety.
chess.faq_diff: How do I choose the AI difficulty?
chess.faq_diff_a: Level 1 is for complete beginners. Levels 2–3 require basic strategy. Level 4 (Hard) calculates several moves ahead.
chess.faq_login: Do I need an account to save results?
chess.faq_login_a: No — it's optional. Log in to save your match history and rank points, or simply play as a guest.
chess.feat1: Complete rules: castling, en passant and promotion all included
chess.feat2: AI opponent: 4 difficulty levels from beginner to advanced
chess.feat3: Real-time play: friend matches + random matchmaking
chess.feat4: Hint system: beginner friendly, click to show legal moves
chess.feat5: Move history: replay the full game to review
chess.piece_bishop_desc: Moves any number of squares diagonally, staying on one color for life
chess.piece_board_desc: An 8×8 board of alternating light and dark squares
chess.piece_king_desc: Moves one square in any direction
chess.piece_knight_desc: Moves in an L-shape — the only piece that can jump over others
chess.piece_pawn_desc: Moves forward, captures diagonally; promotion and en passant apply
chess.piece_queen_desc: The strongest piece — moves any number of squares in any direction
chess.piece_rook_desc: Moves any number of squares horizontally or vertically
chess.what_is_desc: Chess is the world's most popular strategy board game. It originated in 6th-century India as Chaturanga, traveled through Persia to Europe, and took its modern form there. Two players maneuver pieces on an 8×8 board to attack the opponent's king — checkmate wins. Chess is an Olympic sport and the first board game where AI surpassed the human world champion.

tictactoe.faq_expand: Can it expand to bigger boards?
tictactoe.faq_expand_a: Yes! This site also has a 3×3 math version (Sum=15) plus 4×4 and 5×5 connection variants.
tictactoe.faq_win_a: With perfect play from both sides the game is always a draw. If X blunders, O can win — and vice versa.
tictactoe.hp1: Pick a mode: AI, friend or random match
tictactoe.hp2: X moves first — click an empty square
tictactoe.hp3: O moves next (or the AI responds)
tictactoe.hp4: Block your opponent's threats while creating your own
tictactoe.rule1: 3×3 grid, X moves first, O second
tictactoe.rule2: Take turns marking empty squares; marks never move
tictactoe.rule4: Grid full with no winner is a draw
tictactoe.strat1_desc: Opening in a corner raises your win rate — it guarantees at least a draw. Opening in the center can lose depending on O's reply.
tictactoe.strat2_desc: The moment your opponent places two marks on one line, block the third square immediately!
tictactoe.strat3_desc: Threaten two winning lines at once — your opponent can block only one, and you win. This is tic-tac-toe's core tactic.
tictactoe.what_is_desc: Tic-Tac-Toe is the world's simplest classic two-player game. On a 3×3 grid, two players alternate placing X and O; the first to connect three horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins. It's the perfect introduction to game theory — perfect play from both sides always ends in a draw.

gomoku.faq_diff: How do I choose the AI difficulty?
gomoku.faq_diff_a: Easy: random + simple heuristics for beginners. Normal: evaluation + shallow search. Medium: threat-space search. Hard: locally optimal moves for advanced players.
gomoku.faq_forbidden_a: To offset black's first-move advantage, black is restricted: no double-threes, double-fours or overlines (six or more), or black loses. This can be toggled in settings.
gomoku.faq_undo_a: Yes — long-press the board or tap the undo button to take back one move.
gomoku.play1: Pick a mode: AI, friend or random match
gomoku.play2: Click an intersection to place a stone — black moves first
gomoku.play3: Watch your opponent and read 2–3 moves ahead
gomoku.play4: Create open threes and fours to force your opponent to defend
gomoku.play5: First to line up five stones wins
gomoku.rule2: Stones go on intersections — once placed they never move
gomoku.skill1_desc: A four is a threat that must be blocked (or your opponent wins next move). An open three is one step from a four — mastering these shapes is gomoku's foundation.
gomoku.skill2_desc: Create two open threes (or fours) at once — your opponent can only block one, locking in the win.
gomoku.skill3_desc: The center point is worth the most. After every move ask: in how many directions can this stone grow?
gomoku.what_is_desc: Gomoku (Five in a Row) is a classic two-player strategy game popular across East Asia. Black and white alternate placing stones on a 15×15 board; the first to line up five horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins. The rules are simple but the strategy runs deep — a minute to learn, a lifetime to master.

connect4.faq_diff: How many AI difficulty levels are there?
connect4.faq_diff_a: Three: Easy (1–2 ply lookahead), Normal (4–6 ply) and Hard (7+ ply with an evaluation function).
connect4.faq_draw: Can Connect Four end in a draw?
connect4.faq_draw_a: In theory yes (the board fills with no winner), but it's extremely rare at higher levels — the first player usually wins.
connect4.faq_mobile_a: Fully. The responsive design adapts to phones and tablets — just tap a column to drop a piece.
connect4.play1: Pick a mode: AI, friend or random match
connect4.play2: Click the arrow above a column to drop a piece
connect4.play3: The piece falls to the lowest empty slot in that column
connect4.play4: Look for four-in-a-row horizontally, vertically or diagonally
connect4.play5: Build your own line while blocking your opponent's
connect4.rule2: Pieces fall automatically to the lowest empty slot
connect4.rule4: Board full with no winner is a draw
connect4.strat1_desc: The center column (column 4) participates in the most winning lines — controlling it is the key to the board. Research shows players who own over 70% of center cells almost always win.
connect4.strat2_desc: Build two three-in-a-rows at once — your opponent can only block one, locking in the win.
connect4.strat3_desc: Drop pieces low to leave room for connections above. Fill the bottom rows first, then play upward.
connect4.what_is_desc: Connect Four is a classic two-player strategy game first sold by Milton Bradley in 1974. It's played on a vertical 7×6 board where pieces fall from the top and stack up. Players take turns dropping pieces; the first to connect four horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins. Simple on the surface, but solved by algorithms — research proved the first player has a winning strategy.

othello.faq_diff: Othello vs Go — what's the difference?
othello.faq_diff_a: Completely different. Go is about claiming territory; Othello flips your opponent's discs. Othello has simple rules with deep strategy, while Go has minimal rules with endless depth.
othello.faq_no_moves: Why can I run out of legal moves?
othello.faq_no_moves_a: If no move can sandwich an opponent disc, you must pass. The game automatically shows Pass.
othello.hp1: Black moves first automatically — click a highlighted legal square
othello.hp2: Your new disc must sandwich at least one opponent disc together with one of your own
othello.hp3: All sandwiched opponent discs flip to your color automatically
othello.hp4: Look for the highlighted legal moves on the board
othello.hp5: If you have no legal move, your turn passes automatically
othello.rule1: 8×8 board with four discs in the center, two black and two white on diagonals
othello.rule2: A move must sandwich at least one opponent disc in a straight line (horizontal, vertical or diagonal)
othello.rule3: All sandwiched opponent discs flip to your color
othello.rule4: No legal move means you pass; the game ends when neither side can move
othello.rule5: Whoever has more discs at the end wins
othello.strat1_desc: The four corners can never be flipped — they're permanently safe. Grab them whenever possible.
othello.strat2_desc: Edge discs are safer — only three sides are exposed. Prefer edges over central squares.
othello.strat3_desc: Flip few discs early and secure good positions; save mass flips for the endgame. First 20 moves: prioritize placement, not count.
othello.strat4_desc: Discs anchored on both sides by your own discs can never be flipped. Build stable formations.
othello.what_is_desc: Othello (Reversi) is a deeply strategic two-player board game. It originated in 19th-century England and became a worldwide hit after being commercialized in Japan in 1971. Players alternate placing discs on an 8×8 board, flipping straight lines of opponent discs. The one with more discs at the end wins — position matters more than count.

checkers.multi_jump_desc: After a jump, if more captures are available, they continue automatically until none are left.
checkers.promote_desc: Reach the opposite row to be crowned a King (👑) that can move and capture backwards.
checkers.rule1: 8×8 board, 12 pieces per side placed on dark squares
checkers.rule2: Regular pieces move diagonally forward one square
checkers.rule3: Capture: jump over an adjacent opponent piece into the empty square beyond
checkers.rule4: Multi-jump: complete all possible captures in one turn
checkers.rule5: Forced capture: if you can capture, you must
checkers.rule6: Kinging: reach the far row to become a King that moves and captures backwards
checkers.strat1_desc: The central 4×4 area controls the most directions. Occupy it to limit your opponent's moves.
checkers.strat2_desc: Before each move ask: if my piece gets taken, can I take back? Don't give away pieces for nothing.
checkers.strat3_desc: Kings move in all directions and are far more flexible. Push pieces to the far row as early as possible.
checkers.what_is_desc: Checkers (Draughts) is one of the world's oldest board games, dating back to ancient Egypt around 3000 BC. It is played only on the dark squares of an 8×8 board, with 12 pieces per side. Pieces move diagonally and capture by jumping over opponents. Win by capturing all enemy pieces or leaving your opponent with no moves.
checkers.win_condition_desc: You win by capturing all of your opponent's pieces or leaving them without a legal move.
